# Module 6 - Statistical Analysis

## Assignment context
This module applies statistical tests to validate hypotheses and find more reliable relationships in the data, using the same dataset as the previous modules. This repository holds **Option A: basic statistical tests** of the hypotheses formed in Module 4.

## Files
| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `statistical_analysis.ipynb` | Pairwise t-tests between customer segments and Pearson correlations |

**Data:** reads `data/processed/mall_customers_clean.csv`, generated by [`module-03-data-cleaning/data_cleaning.ipynb`](../module-03-data-cleaning/data_cleaning.ipynb) (a copy is included). The notebook is committed with its outputs.

## Analysis 1 - Spending score across segment pairs
- **Question:** Which pairs of customer segments have a statistically significant difference in mean spending score?
- **Test:** Independent-samples t-test applied pairwise to all 10 segment pairs. It is a simple, transparent way to see exactly which segments differ without using a more advanced test such as ANOVA.
- **Result:** 8 of 10 pairs have p-values close to zero, so their mean spending scores differ significantly. The two exceptions (p > 0.05):

| Pair | p-value | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Low income / low score vs High income / low score | 0.214 | Income differs but "low" spending behavior is similar |
| Low income / high score vs High income / high score | 0.294 | Income differs but "high" spending behavior is similar |

- **Conclusion:** The segmentation is valid and separates customers by shopping behavior. In several cases the spending category (high / low) is a stronger differentiator than income level.

## Analysis 2 - Factors related to spending score
- **Question:** Are annual income and age linearly correlated with spending score?
- **Test:** Pearson correlation.

| Pair | Correlation (r) | p-value | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Annual income vs spending score | 0.0099 | 0.8890 | No significant correlation overall (without segmentation) |
| Age vs spending score | -0.3272 | < 0.0001 | Weak-to-moderate negative correlation: spending score tends to fall as age increases |

- **Conclusion:** Age has a significant relationship with spending score. Income, taken overall, does not.

## Data limitations
Hypothesis 2 from Module 4 (high-income, low-score customers prioritize saving) cannot be tested directly because the dataset has no variables such as savings amount, investments, or asset ownership. Future work should collect data on financial products or financial goals to validate it.

> Values above match the executed outputs in the notebook. The k-means segment IDs are tied to `random_state=42` on the cleaned data, so verify the cluster-to-name mapping against a scatter plot if your data or library version differs.
